item: a volume restore never writes decrypted data beside the backup, refuses a repeated volume and is bounded by its declared plaintext size (R686)
summary: BEFORE: the legacy oo-volumes-1 reassembly decrypted each volume to <volume>.plain INSIDE the backup folder and removed it after, so a crash or kill in between left plaintext on the user's backup drive, where nothing cleaned it up; it had no free-space preflight, read a volume the manifest listed twice again, and wrote whatever the volumes held. The member-streamed oo-volumes-2 reader likewise read a repeated volume again and was not bounded by the declared plaintext_bytes its staging preflight counted. NOW: the working copy goes beside the reassembled archive in the restore's own .restore-* staging on the data volume (removed on success and failure; the legacy staging now carries its owner's marker like the streamed one's, and .restore-* joined the owner-marked prefixes, so after a crash the next start removes it at once instead of after 24 h); both readers (and verify) refuse, before reading or repairing anything, a manifest that names a volume twice, counting names that differ only by case or a trailing dot or space, a volume that is a link, two names for one file, and a declared size that is negative or not an integer (a negative member size could cancel another out of the staging preflight); legacy volume names must be plain; the legacy reassembly preflights the declared size plus one decrypted volume and stops at the declared size, and each streamed member stops at its own declared size, with a plain message. Copies an interrupted restore left before this release are named by the import scan (only <vol-NNNNN.ooenc>.plain names an oo-volumes-1 manifest in that folder explains, never a listed volume, never a path, drive letter or stream name), the page says so plainly with a caveat, and a Remove button deletes exactly those after a confirm that lists them (relative to a no-follow folder handle where the platform allows), naming any copy it could not remove; nothing is deleted from a backup drive on its own. 22 tests, all but one red on main; two Opus security reads and an Opus correctness read, findings folded (a hard-killed restore leaves no plaintext beside the backup). Release line: An interrupted import can no longer leave unencrypted copies of your backup on the backup drive; if an earlier one did, the import page now tells you and offers to remove them. A damaged or crafted volume backup can no longer make a restore write more than the backup declares.
